title: Split DNS + Regional Egress Stitching: Terraform migration playbook (draft)
summary: Operational playbook to migrate on-prem/VPC deployments to a split-horizon DNS model while stitching regional egress paths via dedicated NAT pools. Contains Terraform module notes, staged upgrade plan, verification checks, and rollback procedures.
content:
Background:

Current problem: several Private deployment customers require deterministic egress IPs per-region for upstream allowlists and centralized network logging. Our existing on-prem and VPC setups use a flat NAT gateway per-cluster with provider-managed DNS. That causes two issues: (1) customers cannot pin predictable egress / source IP ranges per business unit/region, and (2) internal private DNS resolution policy is inconsistent between VPC and on-prem, creating split-horizon surprises for services that expect local internal resolution (e.g., metrics ingestion endpoints).

Goal:
- Introduce a repeatable Terraform-driven pattern that creates region-scoped NAT pools, centralized egress routing (optional BGP or static next-hop), and a split-horizon DNS configuration that keeps private service names resolving to local endpoints while public names resolve out to vendor endpoints.
- Produce a migration playbook with minimal customer downtime and clear verification/rollback steps.

Assumptions and constraints:
- Customers run k8s clusters (EKS/GKE/On-prem k8s) with CNI that supports host-network egress or gateway nodes.
- We can provision cloud NATs for cloud regions and a small fleet of HA edge NAT appliances (VMs) for on-prem stitching.
- Terraform will be the source-of-truth for provisioning NAT, firewall, and DNS resources.
- Changes must be reversible within a maintenance window.

High-level approach (phases):

Phase 0 - Prep and discovery (no infra changes)
- Inventory: list clusters, current egress IPs, associated route tables, and DNS zones. Export to spreadsheet for approval.
- Collect customer allowlists and update contact with expected maintenance windows.
- Create a feature branch in terraform-modules: modules/networking/split-dns-egress.
- Create a canary cluster/environment for test deployments.

Phase 1 - Module rollout (non-prod only)
- Deploy new Terraform modules to canary:
  - module nat_pool: abstractions for allocating static egress IP ranges (cloud_nat_address pools or on-prem equivalent VM nat pairs).
  - module egress_route: creates route table entries and optional BGP configs to prefer nat_pool appliances.
  - module private_dns: creates split-horizon DNS records (private zone with local A records; public forwarding rules for vendor names).
- Verify: outbound connections from canary originate from nat_pool IP range; private DNS resolves local endpoints only.

Phase 2 - Staged region rollout (prod-safe)
- Target one region/customer subset at a time. Apply modules in three steps: provisioning, traffic steering, DNS cutover.
  Step A: Provision NAT pool and firewall ACLs (Terraform apply)
    - Reserve static IPs (cloud or VM elastic IPs).
    - Create firewall rules that allow required egress ports from cluster CIDR to NAT appliances.
  Step B: Traffic steering (gradual)
    - Modify route table with lower-priority new routes pointing to NAT appliance. Use weighted routing (if supported) or ephemeral routes to push 10-20% traffic initially.
    - Run continuous traffic tests (see verification section).
  Step C: DNS cutover
    - Update private_dns module: create local A records for service.example.internal -> local service IPs. Update resolver order on nodes (e.g., systemd-resolved, kubelet resolvConf changes) to prefer internal zone.

Phase 3 - Cleanup and hardening
- Remove old NAT artifacts and outdated routes once confident.
- Tighten firewall policies: lock down to known destinations and ports.
- Update runbooks and add CloudWatch/Prometheus alerts for egress anomalies.

Terraform module notes (module contract and recommended variables)
- modules/networking/split-dns-egress/variables.tf (conceptual):
  - variable region (string)
  - variable cluster_cidr (string)
  - variable nat_pool_size (number, default 4)
  - variable nat_type (enum: [cloud, vm])
  - variable allowed_egress_ports (list(number))
  - variable dns_private_zone_name (string)
  - variable dns_forwarders (list(string))

- modules/networking/split-dns-egress/outputs.tf (conceptual):
  - output nat_addresses (list(string))
  - output nat_gateway_ids (list(string))
  - output private_zone_id (string)

Implementation notes and gotchas:
- On cloud providers, allocate IPs in the same region to avoid cross-region egress charges.
- For on-prem NAT VMs, ensure hairpin NAT behavior is enabled if nodes need to talk to services via the public egress IP.
- DNS resolver order: if customer environment uses DHCP-provided resolvers, coordinate DHCP options changes carefully; prefer to add a local stub resolver on edge nodes that forwards to private zone.
- Kubernetes: watch for kube-dns caching TTLs — set short TTLs (30s) for initial cutover to avoid stale resolution.
- Firewall stateful behavior: adding NAT appliances may change source port translation semantics — test long-lived TCP connections (e.g., model serving streams).

Suggested Terraform resource patterns (examples for AWS/GCP/on-prem):
- AWS cloud_nat style (conceptual snippet):
  resource "aws_eip" "nat_pool" {
    count = var.nat_pool_size
    vpc = true
  }
  resource "aws_nat_gateway" "pool" {
    count = var.nat_pool_size
    allocation_id = aws_eip.nat_pool[count.index].id
    subnet_id = module.subnets.egress_subnet_id
  }

- GCP cloud_nat style (conceptual snippet):
  resource "google_compute_address" "nat_pool" {
    count = var.nat_pool_size
    region = var.region
  }
  resource "google_compute_router_nat" "cloud_nat" {
    name = "redwood-cloud-nat-${var.region}"
    nat_ip_allocate_option = "MANUAL_ONLY"
    nat_ips = google_compute_address.nat_pool.*.address
  }

- On-prem VM pair (conceptual):
  - module virtual_nat_vm {
      source = "../modules/vm-nat"
      count = var.nat_pool_size
      vm_image = var.nat_image
      public_ip = true
    }

Network policy considerations (K8s)
- We recommend adding an egress network policy that restricts pods to only talk to allowed external destinations through the NAT pool. Example YAML (short):

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-egress-to-nat
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443

- Note: above is broad; tighten ipBlock to the NAT appliance IPs for control-plane to appliance traffic. For CNI that supports egress gateways (Istio/Linkerd egress gateway), adapt the policy to force egress via those pods.

Firewall rule checklist
- Source: cluster_cidr, Destination: NAT_pool_IPs, Protocols: TCP/UDP (as needed), Ports: allowed_egress_ports
- Management plane: allow SSH/WinRM to NAT VMs only from ops jump hosts. Disable 0.0.0.0/0 management access.
- Monitoring: open syslog/agent ports to central logging endpoints.

Observability and tests (pre/post):
- Pre-cutover:
  - Baseline latency and throughput to key upstreams (egress latency histogram).\  - Record current egress IPs for each cluster.
- During staged rollouts:
  - Use synthetic traffic generators to test 1k RPS and long-authenticated streams.
  - Validate e2e tracing for select flows.
- Post-cutover:
  - Verify source IP from 5 distinct pods to upstream allowlists.
  - Check DNS resolve from nodes and pods: dig service.example.internal @127.0.0.1 returns local IP.

Rollback plan (if traffic problems detected)
- Immediately revert route table changes to original next-hop (Terraform apply with previous state or use provider-specific quick revert).
- Repoint DNS resolvers back to original configuration and flush caches (kube-dns restart on clusters if needed).
- If NAT VM performance issues: scale down new nat_pool, scale up old NAT gateway, and open high-priority rollback incident channel with customer.

Post-mortem and hardening items to capture after each customer rollout:
- Time to cutover and to rollback, key metrics affected (latency, error rate), and any manual tuning performed.
- Add test cases to terraform-modules CI that simulate route updates and DNS cutovers using local emulation.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Do we want to support BGP over direct circuits for customers with existing SD-WAN? (Marco to validate feasibility with on-prem network team)
- Define SLIs for egress failover (target: <5s failover for route changes).
- Create a small operator (k8s operator or daemonset) that can manage per-node resolver ordering to avoid DHCP changes on customer networks.

Appendix: example verification commands
- Verify egress IP from pod: kubectl exec -it pod/nginx -- curl -s https://ifconfig.co
- Check private DNS resolution: kubectl exec -it pod/dig -- dig +short service.example.internal @10.0.0.53
- Validate route table entries (AWS): aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=tag:Cluster,Values=my-cluster

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working draft focused on networking specifics for Private deployments. Comments welcome on module variable naming, on-prem VM HA patterns, and risk thresholds for staged traffic percentages.
